# PlayLens Masterbrain Prompt
> Canonical project operating document for PlayLens, an AI-native NFL play intelligence system.
> Treat this file as the source of truth for product scope, ML architecture, data contracts, UI behavior, implementation sequencing, quality gates, and future expansion.
> Snapshot date: 2026-09-29.
> Primary build horizon: 14 calendar days, with a small contingency buffer if needed.
> Core principle: build one coherent ML product, not a collection of disconnected demos.
## 0. How an AI Coding Agent Must Use This File
- Read this file before proposing architecture, writing production code, changing a public contract, or introducing a dependency.
- Preserve the eight-feature committed scope unless the user explicitly changes it.
- When a requirement conflicts with a later explicit user instruction, follow the user instruction and record the decision in the Decision Log.
- Prefer a small number of high-quality, testable components over a wide set of incomplete experiments.
- Do not invent metrics, model performance, dataset fields, NFL facts, or external API behavior. Mark unknowns and verify them.
- Do not present LLM-generated explanations as model evidence. Every football-specific analytical claim exposed in the UI must be traceable to structured data, deterministic computation, or an explicitly labeled language-model interpretation.
- Do not silently change data splits, target definitions, normalization conventions, coordinate systems, or evaluation metrics.
- Keep interfaces typed. Treat frontend, backend, model serving, and database boundaries as explicit contracts.
- Prefer reproducibility over cleverness. A result that cannot be recreated from a commit, dataset version, and experiment record is not considered complete.
- Optimize for the final demo path: search/select play -> replay -> inspect model -> similar plays -> compare -> ask analyst -> modify one defender -> rerun -> inspect evaluation evidence.
- When forced to choose between infrastructure polish and user-visible product quality during the two-week build, protect model correctness, frontend polish, and the demo path first.
- Do not introduce Kubernetes, service meshes, Kafka, or multiple deployable microservices during the initial build unless a demonstrated bottleneck requires them.
- Do not turn PlayLens into a betting product, fantasy product, game-winner predictor, injury predictor, or generic NFL chat application.
- Do not use the LLM as a substitute for an unavailable analytical model. If a model capability is not implemented, say so and hide or disable the relevant UI.
- Before merging a feature, update or add tests, metrics, observability, documentation, and a short implementation note.
## 1. Product Thesis
PlayLens is an AI-native NFL play intelligence platform that transforms player-tracking sequences into learned play representations that can be replayed, searched, compared, predicted, explained, and manipulated.
The product is built around one central concept: **a football play is not merely a row of tabular statistics; it is a time-evolving interaction graph.**
PlayLens therefore treats players as interacting entities, tracking frames as temporal observations, and whole plays as learned representations. The resulting representation powers multiple downstream experiences without requiring unrelated one-off models for every screen.
The project exists to answer questions such as:
- What happened spatially during this play?
- Which historical plays developed in a structurally similar way?
- Which player interactions most distinguish this play from similar plays?
- Where did the model expect players to move next?
- How uncertain was that prediction?
- What changes when one defender starts from a different location?
- Can an AI analyst explain the result using PlayLens data and model tools instead of freeform football speculation?
## 2. The Problem PlayLens Solves
- Traditional box-score products collapse a dynamic play into a handful of aggregate outcomes.
- Raw tracking datasets are powerful but difficult to inspect without specialized tooling.
- Similarity is usually defined with manually selected categorical fields rather than learned spatial-temporal structure.
- Trajectory models are often shown only as offline metrics rather than as understandable visual predictions.
- Generative AI can explain sports data fluently, but without grounded tools it can fabricate causes, statistics, or tactical conclusions.
- ML portfolio projects commonly stop at notebooks and metrics, which hides the engineering required to turn models into useful products.
PlayLens addresses all six problems by combining interactive tracking visualization, graph/sequence representation learning, vector retrieval, calibrated prediction, tool-grounded AI, and production-style evaluation inside one coherent product.
## 3. Primary User Experience
The canonical demo must support the following end-to-end path without manual notebook intervention:
1. Open Explore and select or search for a play.
2. Open the Play view and watch the player-tracking sequence animate on a football field.
3. Toggle overlays for trails, velocity, nearest-defender relationships, predicted paths, actual paths, and uncertainty.
4. Inspect the learned play embedding summary and downstream model outputs.
5. Request similar plays and receive vector-retrieved results with transparent metadata filters.
6. Open Compare and synchronize the current play with one retrieved play.
7. Ask the AI Analyst why the plays are similar or different.
8. Observe tool calls backed by structured PlayLens functions rather than freeform claims.
9. Open PlayLab Lite, move one defender at the allowed pre-snap frame, and rerun model inference.
10. Compare original and modified predictions while seeing a visible disclaimer that the experiment is a model counterfactual, not causal proof.
11. Open Evaluation and inspect baseline comparisons, model metrics, retrieval examples, uncertainty/calibration evidence, and inference latency.
## 4. Committed Scope: Exactly Eight Core Features
### F1. Interactive Tracking Replay
Polished field animation with player positions, timeline events, hover details, trails, vectors, relationships, and model overlays.
### F2. GNN/Transformer Play Encoder
A learned spatial-temporal encoder that turns a play into a reusable embedding and supports downstream heads.
### F3. Similarity Search + Compare Mode
pgvector-backed play retrieval plus synchronized, evidence-rich side-by-side comparison.
### F4. Player Trajectory Prediction
Actual versus predicted future movement with uncertainty visualization and robust evaluation.
### F5. Tool-Grounded AI Analyst
An LLM interface that can only make analytical claims using PlayLens tools and returned evidence.
### F6. Generative AI UI
AI responses can produce typed play cards, comparison panels, filters, timeline jumps, and visualization actions.
### F7. PlayLab Lite
Move one defender in a constrained pre-snap scenario and rerun inference for a model-based counterfactual comparison.
### F8. Professional ML Evaluation
A first-class evaluation surface for baselines, learned models, uncertainty, retrieval quality, latency, and reproducibility.
## 5. Non-Goals for the Two-Week Build
- No fantasy lineup optimizer.
- No sports-betting recommendation or wagering edge system.
- No injury prediction.
- No generic game winner predictor.
- No broad NFL news chatbot.
- No sentiment analysis.
- No player ranking leaderboard as a primary product.
- No attempt to infer true defensive play calls unless labels and evaluation support that claim.
- No full coaching simulator.
- No claim that PlayLab establishes causal effects.
- No requirement to support every NFL season in v1.
- No requirement to support live in-game inference in v1.
- No premature multi-region infrastructure.
- No distributed training unless a real training bottleneck requires it.
- No complex event streaming infrastructure merely for resume keywords.
## 6. Success Definition
PlayLens v1 is successful when a reviewer can use the deployed application, understand the product in under one minute, complete the canonical demo path, and inspect enough technical evidence to trust that the ML is real.
The v1 success bar includes:
- A polished and responsive frontend suitable for a portfolio centerpiece.
- A reproducible ML pipeline with explicit training/validation/test policy.
- At least one simple baseline for every learned prediction task.
- A graph/temporal encoder that is actually used by a product feature.
- Vector retrieval driven by learned embeddings, not only hand-crafted metadata.
- Trajectory uncertainty represented numerically and visually.
- Grounded AI tool calls with auditable structured inputs and outputs.
- A constrained but convincing PlayLab experience.
- An evaluation page that exposes wins, losses, limitations, and latency.
- A deployment that can be launched from a clean clone using documented commands.
## 7. 2026 Technology Direction
Use current stable/LTS-compatible releases at implementation time rather than blindly pinning versions in this planning document. As of the project snapshot, Next.js 16 is the active LTS line, Vercel AI SDK 7 is current, MLflow 3.x is current, and pgvector supports HNSW/IVFFlat approximate nearest-neighbor indexes. Record exact selected versions in package manifests and environment files.
Preferred stack:
- **Web application:** Next.js + React + TypeScript
- **UI system:** Tailwind CSS + shadcn/ui + a minimal custom design system
- **Animation / field renderer:** PixiJS or performant Canvas rendering, with SVG only where appropriate
- **AI interaction layer:** Vercel AI SDK 7 or equivalent typed tool-calling layer
- **Backend API:** FastAPI + Pydantic
- **Core ML:** PyTorch
- **Graph ML:** PyTorch Geometric
- **Baselines:** scikit-learn and/or LightGBM
- **Dataframes / feature engineering:** Polars
- **Local analytical queries:** DuckDB
- **Artifact format:** Parquet
- **Operational database:** PostgreSQL
- **Vector retrieval:** pgvector + HNSW
- **Cache / ephemeral state:** Redis only where it gives measurable value
- **Experiment tracking:** MLflow
- **API/model observability:** OpenTelemetry-compatible tracing and structured logs
- **Frontend hosting:** Vercel or equivalent
- **Backend/model hosting:** A simple container platform or cloud VM/service appropriate to GPU/CPU needs
- **Packaging:** Docker
- **CI:** GitHub Actions or equivalent

## 9. Data Strategy
- Use NFL tracking data available under the applicable competition/data-use terms for development and portfolio demonstration.
- Use nflverse or another reliable football data source for compatible play-level metadata where licensing and identifiers permit.
- Create a dataset manifest that records source, version/date, files, row counts, schema hash, checksums, and preprocessing commit.
- Never train on data that accidentally leaks post-outcome information into a pre-outcome prediction target.
- Keep raw data immutable. All normalization and coordinate transformations happen in reproducible derived steps.
- Create a small deterministic development subset so frontend/backend work does not require full-dataset processing.
- Build adapters so the product can later support additional tracking seasons without rewriting all model code.
### 9.1 Canonical Coordinate System
- Normalize plays so offense direction is consistent whenever this improves model invariance and visualization consistency.
- Preserve the original coordinate frame in raw fields for auditability.
- Document field dimensions, units, origin, direction, and all transforms.
- Make coordinate transformation functions pure and unit-tested.
- Never mix normalized and original coordinates in one model batch without explicit field names.
### 9.2 Canonical Play Record
Every play exposed to the application should map to one typed canonical representation with the following conceptual fields:
- play_id and game_id
- season/week/game metadata where available
- down and distance
- quarter and clock context
- possession/offense and defense identifiers
- tracking frames
- frame time/index
- event labels such as snap or throw where available
- player identifier, team side, position/role when available
- x/y location
- speed
- acceleration
- orientation
- movement direction
- ball position where available
- target outcome fields used only when permitted by the task
- data provenance and schema version
## 10. Feature F1: Interactive Tracking Replay
The replay is the visual center of the product. It must feel immediate, readable, and intentional rather than like a scatter plot with a play button.
### 10.1 Core Behavior
- Render all available offensive players, defensive players, and the ball per frame.
- Interpolate animation only for visual smoothness; never silently alter model input frames.
- Support play, pause, seek, step frame, speed controls, and reset.
- Mark important timeline events such as snap, throw, arrival, or catch when available.
- Hover or select a player to expose speed, acceleration, direction, nearest opponent, and separation when computed.
- Keep player identity stable across frames.
- Provide clear visual distinction between offense, defense, ball, predicted path, actual path, and uncertainty.
### 10.2 Overlay Toggles
- player trails
- velocity vectors
- acceleration vectors if useful
- nearest-defender edges
- model interaction edges
- actual future path
- predicted future path
- uncertainty band or sampled futures
- player labels
- selected-player focus
- critical/interesting frame marker
### 10.3 Performance Requirements
- Avoid React re-rendering every player node on every animation tick if Canvas/Pixi state can handle it more efficiently.
- Preload the selected play payload.
- Keep user interactions responsive while animation is running.
- Measure first replay render, play-switch latency, and animation frame performance.
- Degrade gracefully on lower-powered devices by reducing cosmetic effects before removing core information.
## 11. Feature F2: GNN/Transformer Play Encoder
The encoder is the core ML representation learner. It must be architecturally coherent enough to support embeddings, similarity, and trajectory-related downstream tasks without pretending one model solves everything perfectly.
### 11.1 Conceptual Architecture
```text
tracking frame -> player nodes -> interaction graph -> spatial GNN -> frame representation
frame representations -> temporal Transformer -> play representation
play/player representations -> projection head / trajectory decoder / downstream heads
```
### 11.2 Node Features
- normalized x and y position
- speed
- acceleration
- orientation encoded cyclically
- movement direction encoded cyclically
- offense/defense/ball type embedding
- player role/position embedding when available
- relative position to ball
- relative position to line of scrimmage when defined
- frame-relative temporal position
### 11.3 Edge Strategy
- Start with a simple, inspectable graph definition such as k-nearest spatial neighbors plus team/opponent indicators.
- Benchmark graph construction cost.
- Encode relative displacement and distance as edge features.
- Consider offense-defense cross edges explicitly.
- Do not hard-code a claimed coverage relationship unless labels or a validated heuristic support it.
- Expose enough edge semantics to render an interpretable interaction graph in the UI.
### 11.4 Training Objectives
- Use a primary supervised or self-supervised objective that is clearly defined and measurable.
- For similarity-quality representation learning, consider contrastive learning using defensible positive/negative construction.
- For trajectory modeling, use a future-position objective with masks for available players/frames.
- If multi-task training is used, log each task loss separately and tune loss weights explicitly.
- Do not claim embedding semantics merely because nearest neighbors look plausible. Evaluate retrieval quality with human-readable and quantitative checks.
## 12. Feature F3: Similarity Search and Compare Mode
- Persist normalized play embeddings in PostgreSQL using pgvector.
- Use cosine similarity unless experiments justify another distance metric.
- Create an HNSW index for interactive approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval once corpus size warrants it.
- Retain an exact-search mode for offline evaluation of ANN recall.
- Support optional metadata filters such as down, distance band, offense/defense, play family, or temporal slice when those fields are trustworthy.
- Return similarity score/distance, metadata, and retrieval provenance.
- Never present an arbitrary cosine score as a calibrated probability.
### 12.1 Compare Mode
- Render two plays side by side.
- Support synchronized playback by normalized play phase or relative frame index.
- Allow independent scrub as a fallback.
- Show top structural differences such as spacing, nearest-opponent distance, velocity pattern, and selected model-derived descriptors.
- Permit AI Analyst tool calls to reference both play IDs and return explicit evidence.
- Allow a user to jump directly from a comparison explanation to the most relevant frame.
## 13. Feature F4: Player Trajectory Prediction
The trajectory model predicts future player movement from an allowed observed prefix. Exact target windows depend on dataset/task availability and must be documented.
### 13.1 Output Contract
- predicted future x/y path per modeled player
- valid-frame mask
- uncertainty representation
- model version
- input frame window
- prediction horizon
- latency
### 13.2 Uncertainty
- Prefer a probabilistic output, ensemble, quantile/variance head, mixture density formulation, or sampled-future approach that can be defended.
- Do not display uncertainty shading that is not derived from a defined statistical/model quantity.
- Evaluate uncertainty calibration or coverage where possible.
- Make uncertainty visually subordinate to the primary prediction but easy to inspect.
### 13.3 Metrics
- Average displacement error or a clearly defined equivalent.
- Final displacement error or a clearly defined equivalent.
- Per-horizon error curves.
- Per-player-role slices where sample sizes support them.
- Uncertainty coverage/calibration metric when probabilistic output is implemented.
- CPU/GPU inference latency distribution.
## 14. Feature F5: Tool-Grounded AI Analyst
The AI Analyst is an orchestration and explanation layer. It must not become the source of truth for numerical or tactical claims.
### 14.1 Allowed Tool Families
- `get_play(play_id)`
- `get_play_frames(play_id, range)`
- `get_player_state(play_id, player_id, frame)`
- `get_nearest_opponents(play_id, player_id, frame)`
- `get_separation_series(play_id, player_id)`
- `get_play_embedding(play_id)`
- `find_similar_plays(play_id, filters, k)`
- `compare_plays(play_a, play_b)`
- `get_trajectory_prediction(play_id, config)`
- `get_model_metrics(model_version)`
- `run_counterfactual(play_id, modification)`
- `jump_to_frame(play_id, frame) as a UI action`
- `set_overlay(play_id, overlay, state) as a UI action`
### 14.2 Grounding Rules
- If the user asks a numerical question, retrieve the number from a tool or say it is unavailable.
- If the user asks why two plays are similar, call the similarity/compare tools and cite returned feature evidence.
- If a tool returns uncertainty, preserve it in the answer rather than flattening it to certainty.
- Distinguish observed data from model prediction from language-model interpretation.
- Avoid causal verbs unless the analysis is actually causal.
- Return structured evidence IDs with each analytical response so the UI can display provenance.
- Do not expose hidden chain-of-thought. Provide concise user-facing rationale and evidence only.
## 15. Feature F6: Generative AI UI
AI responses may produce typed UI artifacts rather than only text. Every generated component must map to a strict schema controlled by the application.
### 15.1 Supported Generated UI Primitives
- PlayCard
- SimilarPlayList
- ComparisonCard
- MetricTable
- TimelineJump
- OverlayToggleAction
- PlayerFocusAction
- TrajectorySummary
- CounterfactualSummary
- EvaluationMetricCard
- ClarificationPrompt when essential
### 15.2 Generative UI Safety
- The model chooses among known components; it does not generate arbitrary executable frontend code.
- Validate every tool input and generated component payload against a schema.
- Treat unknown component types as invalid.
- Require explicit user action for state-changing counterfactual modifications.
- Never let the LLM directly write SQL or execute arbitrary backend code in production.
## 16. Feature F7: PlayLab Lite
PlayLab Lite is intentionally constrained. The initial version allows a user to select one eligible defender, reposition that player within a valid region at a permitted pre-snap frame, and rerun the available model pipeline.
### 16.1 V1 Interaction
- Pause at the configured editable frame.
- Select one defender.
- Drag to a valid field coordinate.
- Display original position as a ghost marker.
- Validate maximum displacement and field bounds.
- Submit the modified input to a dedicated counterfactual endpoint.
- Render original and modified predictions together.
- Display a persistent label: model counterfactual, not causal inference.
- Allow reset to original play.
### 16.2 PlayLab Non-Claims
- Do not call the result an optimal defensive alignment.
- Do not claim a team would have prevented or caused an outcome.
- Do not claim coaching validity.
- Do not extrapolate outside the model training distribution without warning.
## 17. Feature F8: Professional ML Evaluation
Evaluation is a product feature, not a hidden notebook. It demonstrates model credibility and engineering maturity.
### 17.1 Required Evaluation Sections
- Dataset and split summary.
- Baseline definitions.
- Learned model definitions.
- Trajectory metrics.
- Uncertainty metrics.
- Similarity/retrieval qualitative examples.
- ANN recall and latency if approximate retrieval is enabled.
- Inference latency p50/p95/p99 where enough samples exist.
- Error slices.
- Model limitations.
- Experiment/model version links or IDs.
## 18. Baselines Before Complexity
- A trivial constant-velocity trajectory extrapolator is a valuable baseline.
- A lightweight MLP/LSTM/temporal baseline may be useful before the full GNN/Transformer.
- A metadata-only similarity baseline should be compared against learned embeddings.
- Exact nearest-neighbor search should benchmark approximate HNSW behavior.
- If a complex model cannot beat a simple baseline on the chosen metric and split, do not hide it. Diagnose it.
## 19. Data Splitting and Leakage Policy
- Prefer game-level or temporal splits over random frame-level splits.
- Prevent frames from the same play appearing across train and evaluation partitions.
- For retrieval evaluation, prevent trivial self-match.
- Document whether the same players or teams can appear across splits.
- If time-based generalization is a goal, train on earlier data and validate/test on later data.
- Any target-dependent feature must be unavailable before the target time for pre-outcome tasks.
## 20. Model Reproducibility Contract
- Every training run records git commit.
- Every training run records config.
- Every training run records dataset manifest/hash.
- Every training run records random seed policy.
- Every training run records dependency/environment information.
- Every training run records metrics.
- Every deployable model has a version and model card.
- Inference responses include model version.
- Evaluation artifacts can be traced back to the run that created them.
## 21. API Design Principles
- Version public APIs under /api/v1 during v1.
- Use Pydantic models for all request/response contracts.
- Return stable IDs, not frontend-specific object references.
- Separate user errors from server/model errors.
- Include model version and latency metadata on inference responses.
- Use pagination for browse/search lists.
- Avoid giant all-frames payloads when a range or compressed representation is sufficient.
- Document every endpoint in generated OpenAPI and keep examples valid.
### 21.1 Proposed Endpoints
- `GET /api/v1/plays`
- `GET /api/v1/plays/{play_id}`
- `GET /api/v1/plays/{play_id}/frames`
- `GET /api/v1/plays/{play_id}/embedding`
- `POST /api/v1/search/similar`
- `POST /api/v1/compare`
- `POST /api/v1/predict/trajectory`
- `POST /api/v1/playlab/counterfactual`
- `GET /api/v1/models`
- `GET /api/v1/evaluation/summary`
- `POST /api/v1/analyst/tools/{tool_name} where appropriate behind internal orchestration`
## 22. Database Design
- plays table for stable play metadata.
- players table or stable player reference layer where allowed/needed.
- play_embeddings table keyed by play_id and model_version.
- model_versions table with semantic metadata.
- evaluation_runs table for surfaced reports if not read directly from experiment storage.
- counterfactual_sessions or ephemeral objects only if persistence is useful.
- AI interaction traces stored with privacy-conscious retention if observability is enabled.
### 22.1 Example Embedding Table
```sql
CREATE TABLE play_embeddings (
  play_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  model_version TEXT NOT NULL,
  embedding vector(512) NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (play_id, model_version)
);
```
## 23. Frontend Information Architecture
- /explore - play discovery and search.
- /play/[id] - replay and model analysis.
- /compare?left=...&right=... - synchronized comparison.
- /playlab/[id] - constrained counterfactual workspace.
- /evaluation - model and system credibility page.
## 24. Visual Design Direction
- Dark, editorial analytics aesthetic.
- Use a restrained neutral palette; field green is contextual, not the entire brand.
- Use consistent spacing, radius, border, and typography tokens.
- Prefer large visual hierarchy and whitespace over dashboard clutter.
- Use motion to explain state transitions, not as decoration.
- Keep statistics readable and avoid excessive glassmorphism.
- Make the football field the primary visual object on Play and Compare pages.
- Use skeleton states that preserve final layout to avoid jumps.
- Use accessible contrast and keyboard states.
## 25. Frontend State Model
- URL should capture play identity and major shareable state where practical.
- Replay clock belongs to local view state.
- Overlay toggles belong to local/session state.
- Server data should use a query/cache layer rather than ad-hoc effects.
- AI-generated actions must dispatch through typed reducers/actions, not arbitrary DOM manipulation.
- PlayLab modifications must be separable from source play data.
## 26. AI Analyst System Prompt Contract
A production system prompt should convey the following rules:
- You are PlayLens Analyst, an evidence-grounded football analysis assistant.
- Use PlayLens tools for play-specific facts, metrics, model outputs, comparisons, and counterfactuals.
- Do not invent unavailable statistics or coaching intent.
- Separate observed tracking evidence, model prediction, and interpretation.
- When uncertainty or model limitations affect the answer, state them concisely.
- Prefer specific evidence such as frame numbers, distances, trajectories, retrieval scores, or model outputs when available.
- Never describe a counterfactual as causal truth.
- When a user asks for a UI action that exists, emit the typed action rather than explaining how to click it.
## 27. AI Tool Result Envelope
Every analytical tool should return a consistent envelope with enough provenance for downstream display:
```json
{
  "tool": "compare_plays",
  "schema_version": "1",
  "request_id": "...",
  "data": {},
  "evidence": [],
  "model_version": null,
  "warnings": [],
  "latency_ms": 0
}
```
## 28. Observability
- Structured request logs with request ID.
- Trace AI analyst calls from user message -> model step -> tool call -> API/model inference.
- Record model inference latency.
- Record vector search latency and result count.
- Record frontend performance signals that materially affect replay experience.
- Never log secrets or unnecessarily sensitive content.
- Create a simple health endpoint and readiness check.
## 29. Security and Reliability
- Validate every API payload.
- Rate-limit expensive inference/AI endpoints if exposed publicly.
- Keep secrets only in environment/secret management, never git.
- Do not allow generated AI content to bypass typed backend authorization/validation.
- Use read-only database roles where possible for retrieval services.
- Use timeouts on model and LLM calls.
- Handle external model-provider failures gracefully.
- Return deterministic fallback UI when the AI analyst is unavailable; core replay/search should still work.
## 30. Testing Strategy
- Unit tests for coordinate transforms.
- Unit tests for frame ordering.
- Unit tests for graph construction.
- Unit tests for masks/padding.
- Unit tests for metrics.
- Unit tests for counterfactual validation.
- Contract tests for FastAPI response schemas.
- Integration tests for play -> embedding -> pgvector retrieval.
- Integration tests for analyst -> tool -> result envelope.
- Frontend component tests for replay controls and generative UI schemas.
- End-to-end test for the canonical demo path.
- Golden visual or snapshot tests only where they add value and are stable.
- Regression test for a few known plays used in the demo.
## 31. ML Testing
- Shape tests for every model forward path.
- NaN/Inf detection.
- Mask correctness tests.
- Overfit-a-tiny-batch sanity test.
- Deterministic inference test under a fixed seed where supported.
- Baseline metric regression thresholds.
- Embedding normalization/distance sanity checks.
- Retrieval self-match exclusion test.
- Counterfactual out-of-distribution warning test.
## 32. Performance Budgets
Set budgets early and revise them only with evidence. Initial targets are engineering goals, not guaranteed claims:
- Cached play metadata response should feel effectively immediate.
- Replay data should load fast enough that a user does not lose context when switching among similar plays.
- Vector search should target interactive latency at the chosen corpus size.
- Trajectory inference should target an interaction-friendly latency on the selected deployment hardware.
- AI analyst should stream partial output when appropriate rather than block on a long final response.
- PlayLab should make progress/state visible if inference is slower than normal replay interactions.
## 33. Experiment Tracking with MLflow
- Create separate experiments for trajectory baselines, encoder/representation runs, and retrieval evaluation if that improves organization.
- Log hyperparameters, dataset manifest ID, code revision, metrics, artifacts, and model signatures.
- Register candidate models only after passing evaluation gates.
- Use clear aliases such as candidate and production only if actual deployment workflow needs them.
- Link model cards to MLflow run/model identifiers.
- Use MLflow tracing/evaluation for AI interactions only if it fits the schedule; do not let observability scope consume the core product build.
## 34. CI/CD
- Lint and typecheck frontend.
- Run Python formatting/linting/type checks.
- Run unit tests.
- Run contract tests.
- Build frontend.
- Build backend container.
- Do not run expensive full training in standard CI.
- Optionally run a tiny smoke-training job on a miniature dataset.
- Protect the main branch with required checks once the repo is stable.

## 36. Daily Shipping Rule
- Every day must end with at least one runnable increment.
- Do not spend multiple consecutive days only on model experiments without integrating a usable candidate into the product.
- Use feature flags or mock adapters early, but replace them with real model outputs before considering a feature complete.
- Keep a single demo fixture collection of plays that exercises the major UI states.
## 37. Definition of Done for a Feature
- User-facing behavior implemented.
- Typed interface defined.
- Backend/model behavior implemented.
- Loading state implemented.
- Error state implemented.
- Tests added.
- Metrics or telemetry added where relevant.
- Accessibility considered.
- Documentation updated.
- No hard-coded fake production data.
- Feature works in deployed environment.
- Feature supports the canonical demo path.
## 38. Model Card Template
- Model name and version.
- Intended use.
- Non-intended use.
- Training data and date/version.
- Input representation.
- Target definition.
- Architecture.
- Baseline.
- Primary metrics.
- Slice metrics.
- Uncertainty behavior.
- Known limitations.
- Out-of-distribution concerns.
- Inference hardware.
- Latency.
- Reproducibility identifiers.
- Owner/last update.
## 39. Decision Log Template
Use `docs/decisions/ADR-XXXX-title.md` with:
- Context
- Decision
- Alternatives considered
- Why this choice
- Consequences
- Revisit trigger
- Date
- Relevant commit/PR
## 40. Demo Script
1. Open Explore and choose a prepared play with visually clear movement.
2. Open Play and begin replay.
3. Toggle trails and nearest-defender edges.
4. Enable trajectory prediction and show actual versus predicted movement with uncertainty.
5. Click Find Similar Plays.
6. Open the top meaningful retrieval result.
7. Switch to Compare and synchronize the plays.
8. Ask the analyst: Why are these plays similar?
9. Show that the analyst calls structured tools and cites play/model evidence.
10. Jump to a relevant frame from the generated UI action.
11. Open PlayLab Lite, move one defender, and rerun.
12. Compare original versus modified model predictions.
13. Open Evaluation and show baseline comparison, error metrics, retrieval examples, and latency.
## 41. Portfolio Story
The project should support a concise technical story:
"I built PlayLens, an AI-native NFL play intelligence platform over player-tracking data. I represented each tracking frame as a player interaction graph, encoded spatial relationships with a GNN and temporal behavior with a Transformer, then used the learned play embeddings for vector similarity search in Postgres/pgvector. I also trained a trajectory prediction head with uncertainty, built synchronized play comparison and a constrained counterfactual lab, and exposed the models through FastAPI. The AI analyst uses typed tools over those model outputs rather than freeform sports knowledge, and the frontend renders interactive generative UI in Next.js."
## 42. Future Expansion: High-Value ML
- Multi-modal pretraining across tracking, play text, and video if licensing permits.
- Masked trajectory modeling or other self-supervised pretraining.
- Learned route concept discovery.
- Coverage/man-zone representation learning with labeled evaluation.
- Diffusion or flow-based multi-modal trajectory forecasting.
- Heterogeneous graphs with richer player/ball node types.
- Hierarchical possession/drive/game representations.
- Opponent-tendency conditional models.
- Player-style embeddings and similarity.
- Transfer learning across seasons.
- Uncertainty-aware OOD detection for PlayLab modifications.
- Causal analysis only if appropriate assumptions/data/design make it defensible.
## 43. Future Expansion: Product
- Saved play collections and shareable analysis links.
- Coach/analyst workspaces with annotations.
- Natural-language hybrid search across play metadata and learned embeddings.
- Team tendency dashboards built from the same embedding space.
- Route/coverage cluster explorer.
- Player comparison surfaces.
- Notebook/export API for researchers.
- Mobile/tablet-friendly film-room mode.
- Collaborative comments.
- Live or near-live ingestion if reliable/licensed tracking becomes available.
## 44. Future Expansion: Systems
- Dedicated model-serving runtime only when concurrency or hardware utilization requires it.
- Batch embedding jobs with queue/orchestration once corpus refreshes become substantial.
- Object storage for large derived artifacts.
- Feature store only if offline/online feature skew becomes a real operational problem.
- GPU autoscaling if public inference load warrants it.
- Streaming data plane only if live ingestion becomes a product requirement.
- Multi-region deployment only if user geography and availability needs justify it.
## 45. Future Expansion: Research Questions
- What similarity objective best corresponds to human football similarity judgments?
- Do graph edges based on spatial nearest-neighbors outperform learned attention-only interaction for this dataset?
- How much performance comes from absolute spatial features versus relational features?
- How stable are play embeddings across model seeds?
- How does embedding neighborhood quality change across seasons or teams?
- Which uncertainty method is best calibrated for trajectory forecasting?
- Can counterfactual modifications be detected as out-of-distribution before inference?
- Can a self-supervised encoder reduce labeled-data dependence for downstream tasks?
## 46. Scope Cut Order if Time Runs Short
1. Do not cut basic replay correctness.
2. Do not cut baselines/evaluation credibility.
3. Do not cut learned embedding retrieval if the project is still called PlayLens.
4. Do not cut tool grounding from the AI Analyst.
5. Reduce the number of generative UI component types before removing generative UI entirely.
6. Make PlayLab support only one prepared modification type rather than generalizing it.
7. Reduce visual overlay count before adding infrastructure complexity.
8. Use a smaller data corpus before compromising data correctness.
## 47. Questions an AI Agent Must Ask Itself Before Adding a Dependency
- Does an existing dependency already solve this?
- Does this dependency materially improve the two-week product?
- Is it actively maintained and compatible with selected runtime versions?
- Can the team explain why it is present?
- Does it add a service that now needs observability, credentials, or deployment?
- What is the removal cost if it becomes unnecessary?
## 48. Anti-Hallucination Rules for Project Documentation
- Never write a benchmark number until it has been measured.
- Never call a model state of the art unless a defensible comparison supports that statement.
- Never claim a production user count that does not exist.
- Never claim real-time behavior until latency has been measured in the deployed environment.
- Never claim a football concept label unless it is present in the data or validated by a documented method.
- Never call vector similarity a probability.
- Never call a what-if model output a causal effect.
## 49. Masterbrain Coding Style
- Prefer clear names over clever abstractions.
- Prefer small pure transformation functions for data preprocessing.
- Keep model code separate from dataset I/O.
- Keep API schemas separate from database ORM entities.
- Use type hints throughout Python.
- Use strict TypeScript.
- Avoid any in production code.
- Keep comments focused on why, not restating what code says.
- Write docstrings for non-obvious transforms and model inputs/outputs.
- Use config files for experiment parameters rather than scattered literals.
## 50. Canonical Acceptance Scenarios
- **Replay:** Given a valid play, when the user opens Play, then all tracked entities render in correct positions and the timeline can be controlled.
- **Prediction:** Given a valid observed prefix, when trajectory inference runs, then predicted paths, actual paths when available, uncertainty, model version, and latency are returned.
- **Similarity:** Given a play embedding, when retrieval runs, then self-match is excluded and ranked results include distance/score and metadata.
- **Compare:** Given two plays, when Compare opens, then both replays can be synchronized and model-derived differences are available.
- **Analyst:** Given a play-specific question, when the analyst answers, then play-specific claims are supported by tool evidence.
- **Generative UI:** Given a supported analyst action, when the model emits a typed UI payload, then the application validates and renders it safely.
- **PlayLab:** Given an eligible defender modification, when the user reruns the model, then original and modified predictions are shown and labeled as model counterfactuals.
- **Evaluation:** Given a deployed model version, when Evaluation opens, then baseline comparison, prediction metrics, limitations, and latency are visible.

## 52. Cross-System Contract Registry
### C01. Web -> API: request typing
The web client and FastAPI schema must agree on field names, nullability, enums, units, and error envelopes.
### C02. API -> ML: inference input
The API must convert validated domain inputs into a versioned ML inference request without silently changing units or coordinates.
### C03. ML -> API: prediction output
The ML layer returns typed arrays/metadata that the API serializes without losing masks, uncertainty, model version, or warnings.
### C04. API -> Database: persistence
Database writes and reads preserve model version, schema version, and stable identifiers.
### C05. Embedding -> pgvector: vector dimension
All embeddings in one indexed column must match the expected dimension and normalization policy.
### C06. Analyst -> Tools: tool call
Every tool argument is validated and every tool response uses the evidence envelope.
### C07. Tools -> GenUI: render payload
Only known component schemas may be emitted to the frontend renderer.
### C08. PlayLab -> ML: counterfactual input
Modified coordinates are represented separately from source data and carry validation/OOD warnings.
## 53. Failure Mode Registry
- **missing frames:** Reject or mark incomplete play; do not interpolate silently for analytical outputs.
- **out-of-order frames:** Sort only using a documented stable frame key and validate uniqueness.
- **missing player metadata:** Use unknown role embeddings/labels rather than inventing position.
- **embedding dimension mismatch:** Fail fast at load/write time.
- **model checkpoint incompatible:** Refuse load and surface actionable version error.
- **pgvector unavailable:** Provide a controlled error or optional development exact-search fallback.
- **LLM unavailable:** Keep replay/search/model features usable and show analyst unavailable state.
- **tool timeout:** Return partial analyst response only if evidence is sufficient; otherwise state the tool failed.
- **PlayLab OOD move:** Warn or reject according to configured threshold.
- **uncertainty unavailable:** Do not render fake confidence shading.
- **unsupported browser:** Fall back to reduced rendering where possible.
- **slow device:** Reduce cosmetic overlay density before sacrificing correctness.
## 54. Issue Template
Every implementation issue should include:
- Problem
- User value
- Scope
- Out of scope
- Dependencies
- Contracts affected
- Implementation notes
- Acceptance criteria
- Tests
- Metrics/observability
- Screenshots or API examples if relevant
- Risks
## 55. Pull Request Template
- What changed?
- Why?
- Which Masterbrain requirements are closed?
- Screenshots/demo
- Tests run
- Model/data version impact
- API/schema impact
- Performance impact
- Known limitations
- Follow-ups
## 56. Final Release Checklist
- [ ] Fresh clone setup works.
- [ ] Environment variables documented.
- [ ] Demo dataset setup documented.
- [ ] Database migration works.
- [ ] Model artifact download/load works.
- [ ] Play page works in production.
- [ ] Similarity retrieval works in production.
- [ ] Compare mode works in production.
- [ ] Trajectory prediction works in production.
- [ ] AI analyst tools work in production.
- [ ] Generative UI schemas reject invalid data.
- [ ] PlayLab works in production.
- [ ] Evaluation page matches deployed model version.
- [ ] No secrets in repository.
- [ ] No fake benchmark numbers.
- [ ] No broken links.
- [ ] No console-breaking errors.
- [ ] Mobile/tablet layout is acceptable.
- [ ] Accessibility basics verified.
- [ ] README contains architecture and demo path.
- [ ] Model limitations visible.
- [ ] License/data-use notes visible.
## 57. Master Instruction to Future Agents
When asked to implement, refactor, debug, document, test, or extend PlayLens, optimize for coherence with this architecture. Do not solve a local task by undermining global contracts. If the requested change creates tension with the two-week v1 scope, explain the tension briefly and implement the smallest architecture-preserving solution. If a future explicit user decision changes this document, update the document so it remains the source of truth.

## 62. Closing Product Principle

PlayLens should feel like one product built around one learned understanding of a football play.

The replay makes the data legible.
The encoder makes the data searchable.
The trajectory model makes the future inspectable.
The AI analyst makes the system conversational without replacing evidence.
PlayLab makes the representation interactive without pretending to prove causality.
Evaluation makes the entire system credible.
**Build the smallest version that delivers all of that exceptionally well.**
